title: Myths and Truths About Tornadoes
summary: Josh and Chuck examine common tornado myths and legends: that tornadoes seek out mobile home parks, that overpasses and underpasses are safe shelter, that opening windows equalizes pressure and protects a house, that bathtubs are safe shelter, that tornadoes avoid cities, that they only happen in North America, and that you can outrun a tornado in a car. They cover why mobile homes suffer more damage, the wind tunnel effect of overpasses, the 2008 Atlanta tornado, the 2011 Oklahoma City (El Reno area) tornadoes and the Fujita scale, tornado Alley and Dixie Alley, and the advice to seek shelter rather than drive. The episode ends with a listener mail about nostalgia in Japan (notasukashi) and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Emily's tornado fascination
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Josh's wife Emily's childhood in Ohio, her interest in tornadoes and the movie Twister, and a viral video of a woman sheltering behind a soda machine. They discuss overpass versus underpass and Josh's family's experiences with tornadoes in north Georgia.

segments.title: Mobile homes and tornadoes
segments.summary: They discuss the myth that tornadoes seek out trailer parks. They explain that mobile homes are lighter, often not anchored to a foundation, and much more likely to be destroyed, and that people in mobile homes are far more likely to die. A Purdue study of transition zones in Indiana is mentioned. Josh offers a speculative static electricity theory, which the hosts acknowledge is unproven.

segments.title: Overpasses and underpasses are not shelter
segments.summary: The hosts explain why overpasses and underpasses are dangerous: they create a wind tunnel effect that speeds wind and funnels debris. They discuss the famous overpass video, which involved a surface inflow jet rather than the tornado itself, and note that parked cars under overpasses can block rescue.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break in the episode before the next segment.

segments.title: Opening windows myth
segments.summary: They cover the old advice to open windows to equalize pressure. They explain that it wastes time, does nothing useful, and can let the wind lift the roof. Josh shares a tangent about giving blood for the first time.

segments.title: Bathtubs as tornado shelter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea that bathtubs are a safe place to shelter. They note that most bathtubs are fiberglass around a wood frame and that the safest spot is an interior room with no exterior walls or windows, such as a closet or interior bathroom.

segments.title: Tornadoes and cities; Oklahoma City and Atlanta
segments.summary: They address the myth that tornadoes avoid cities, attributing it to rural land area. They discuss Oklahoma City tornadoes, the EF5 rating and the Fujita scale history, and the 2008 Atlanta tornado that damaged the Peachtree Plaza Hotel and hit near the Georgia Dome during an SEC tournament, killing one person.

segments.title: Tornadoes around the world, tornado Alley and Dixie Alley
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the US sees far more tornadoes than Europe or other regions, that tornadoes occur on every continent except Antarctica, and that the Great Plains form tornado Alley. They mention Dixie Alley in the Southeast and Florida, with tornadoes more common in late fall there.

segments.title: Why you should not try to outrun a tornado
segments.summary: The hosts explain that tornadoes can change direction, double back, and be wide, so outrunning them in a car is dangerous. They discuss the El Reno tornado of 2013, which was record-wide, and the deaths of storm chasers. They also cite a warning against driving to escape a tornado, and clarify that watches and warnings differ.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener in Tokyo describes the Japanese concept of notasukashi, a pleasant sorrow tied to cherry blossom season, and the hosts sign off with contact information.
